candidates.statement: For some ONTs, it may not be practical to experimentally assess exaggerated pharmacology in 89 toxicology studies. This scenario could occur, for example, if the targeted element is not present 90 in the genome of the test species (e.g., cryptic splice site, indel, or exogenous target) or if the 91 intended pharmacodynamic (PD) effect (e.g., exclusion of a particular exon) would result in a 92 transcript that fundamentally differs from that produced in the patient population (e.g., if exon 93 exclusion causes a frameshift that results in a transcript that encodes an aberrant amino acid 94 sequence or contains a premature stop codon). In these cases, a literature-based weight-of- 95 evidence (WoE) assessment of the potential adverse effects resulting from exaggerated 96 pharmacology should be provided (e.g., data from genetically modified animal models or data 97 from known human diseases). 98

candidates.statement: Given their ability to form Watson-Crick-Franklin base pairs, ONTs have the potential to bind to 102 nontargeted RNA or DNA sequences that share partial or complete complementarity with the 103 base sequence present in the ONT, which can lead to adverse effects in humans that might not be 104 detected in toxicology studies. Therefore, sequence-dependent off-target assessments should be 105 conducted for ONTs using appropriate in silico and in vitro methodologies to identify potential 106 off-target hybridization. 107

candidates.statement: Safety pharmacology evaluations of ONTs should address effects of the drug substance on vital 196 functions. The cardiovascular, respiratory, and central nervous systems are usually considered 197 the vital organ systems that should be studied. 7 Pharmacologically relevant species should be 198 used; however, if there are no pharmacologically relevant species (as defined in section II.B.1 of 199 this guidance), an assessment should still be conducted to assess off-target effects. Safety 200 pharmacology evaluations can be conducted as stand-alone studies or as part of single- or repeat- 201 dose toxicity studies when appropriate and feasible. candidates.statement: Generally, the in vitro human ether-a-go-go-related gene (hERG) assay is not warranted for 207 ONTs belonging to a well-characterized ONT class 8 that has demonstrated negligible ability to 208 inhibit this ion channel. If the target biology or off-target hybridization-dependent activity 209 suggests the potential for affecting hERG expression or function, or if the ONT is known to 210 accumulate in the heart, then a hERG assay may be appropriate. If a hERG assay is conducted, it 211 is important to consider the time required to see an ONT-mediated change in protein 212 level/function in the assay cell line when designing the protocol. 9 In vivo cardiovascular safety 213 pharmacology assessments should be conducted for all ONTs before clinical administration. 214

candidates.statement: Appropriate dosing frequency and duration of the toxicity study should consider aspects of drug 299 distribution and half-life, as well as the clinical dosing regimen. The half-life of ONTs can be 300 shorter in animals than humans; consequently, dosing in animals can be more frequent than in 301 humans to ensure sufficient drug exposure. However, more frequent dosing in shorter duration 302 nonclinical studies is generally not sufficient to address effects from a similar number of doses in 303 clinical trials of longer duration. Given the generally prolonged half-life of ONTs at the site of 304 action (in tissues), the onset of PD activity may be delayed, and the duration of the PD effect of 305 an ONT may be prolonged. Consequently, parameters such as distribution phase plasma 306 exposure may not correlate to PD activity. In such cases, PD biomarkers may provide 307 information useful for designing appropriate dosing frequency in toxicity studies. 308

candidates.statement: The first-in-human dose in healthy volunteers should be selected using the general principles 331 outlined in the guidance for industry Estimating the Maximum Safe Starting Dose in Initial 332 Clinical Trials for Therapeutics in Adult Healthy Volunteers (July 2005). In general, a 333 reasonable starting dose can be defined as one that is expected to result in no more than one- 334 tenth of the exposure observed at the no observed adverse effect level in the most relevant (or 335 more sensitive) species and is typically estimated by calculating a human equivalent dose of the 336 animal dose normalized to body surface area. For severe, irreversible, or unmonitorable toxicity 337 it may be more appropriate to use a larger safety margin. Alternative approaches to calculation of 338 the human equivalent dose may be appropriate for some classes of ONTs or routes of 339 administration (e.g., intrathecal dose normalized by cerebrospinal fluid volume) with scientific 340 justification. 341

candidates.statement: The assessment of developmental and reproductive toxicity (DART) for ONTs should be 372 conducted in accordance with the ICH guidance for industry S5(R3) Detection of Reproductive 373 and Developmental Toxicity for Human Pharmaceuticals (May 2021). Typically, this assessment 374 relies on animal studies that assess effects on fertility and early embryonic development, 375 embryofetal development (EFD), and pre- and postnatal development (PPND) endpoints. 376 Fertility and early embryonic development and PPND studies are routinely conducted in rodents, 377 whereas two species, typically rodents and rabbits, are used in EFD studies. There can be cases 378 where the WoE from existing data (e.g., mechanism of action, phenotypic data from genetically 379 modified animals, class effects, general toxicology study results, preliminary EFD study results, 380 human genetic data) can indicate an obvious adverse effect of an ONT on fertility or pregnancy 381 outcome. In these instances, these data may provide adequate information to communicate the 382 risk to reproduction and embryofetal development, and no additional nonclinical studies are 383 warranted. 384

candidates.statement: Although doses and the dosing regimen should generally be selected based on the criteria 386 identified in ICH S5(R3), there can be product- or class-specific attributes of an ONT that may 387 necessitate modifications to the standard DART study designs. In particular, some ONT classes 388 are rapidly cleared from circulation, while having extended tissue residence times and protracted 389 PD effects, which allows for infrequent administration in the clinic. This can pose challenges in 390 the design of the dosing regimen of the DART studies, particularly EFD studies, because the 391 objective of the EFD study is to achieve adequate exposure to both the PD effects and the 392 chemical structure at each stage of organogenesis. Consequently, the dosing regimen for DART 393 studies of ONTs with protracted PK/PD effects is often designed to achieve a balance between 394 ensuring exposure at all stages of development and avoiding clinically irrelevant maternal 395 toxicity resulting from excessive drug exposure or accumulation at the sites of distribution (see 396 note 2). For such products, consultation with the FDA review division regarding appropriate 397 study design is recommended. The approach taken should be scientifically justified. 398

candidates.statement: The effect of the intended pharmacological activity of the ONT on DART endpoints should be 400 assessed. If the clinical candidate is not pharmacologically active in the routine species, an 401 appropriate species-specific surrogate molecule that is active in rodents or rabbits should be 402 used, provided there is sufficient characterization of the model to ensure pharmacological 403 relevance. A typical study design might employ three dose levels of the clinical candidate and a 404 single dose level of the surrogate, though other study designs can be used with justification. The 405 surrogate should generally be dosed at a level that results in the maximal PD effect in the dam. 406 Exposures to the surrogate that exceed the maximal PD effect are not relevant to the safety 407 assessment because these represent off-target activities of an oligonucleotide that will not be 408 administered to humans. Other bases for dose selection for the surrogate (e.g., maximum 409 tolerated dose) may be appropriate with justification. 410

The assessment of immunotoxicity of ONTs should follow ICH and FDA guidance on this 505 topic. 15 Many types of ONTs are known to engage and activate components of the innate 506 immune system (e.g., macrophages, histiocytes, complement). Although stand-alone, dedicated 507 immunotoxicity assessments are not typically warranted, assessment of ONT-induced effects on 508 the immune system (e.g., cytokines, complement) in general toxicity studies can provide useful 509 context for understanding observations seen in these studies. 510

candidates.statement: As for other synthetically derived drug products, impurity levels in ONT drug products should be 555 adequately controlled and demonstrated to be present at levels that do not raise safety concerns. 556 Impurities derived from ONTs can be classified into two broad categories: (1) oligonucleotide- 557 related substances and (2) other impurities (e.g., organic small-molecule impurities, residual 558 solvents, elemental impurities). In the ONT manufacturing process, impurities should be reduced 559 to the lowest practical level and evaluated for safety in humans based on the level of the 560 impurity, existing data about the impurity (including published data), and the results of 561 nonclinical toxicology studies in which the animals are exposed to the impurity. 562
